newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Wessex Water launches share buybacks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Wessex Water launches share buybacks.

text.p: British water group Wessex Water Plc on Wednesday announced a package of share buybacks, making good on a pledge to deliver higher returns to shareholders after a recent bid for South West Water was frustrated.

Wessex, sitting on a healthy cash pile, said it would offer to buy back up to 10 percent of its ordinary shares at 380 pence each in an attempt to simplify its capital structure and increase earnings and dividends.
Its shares traded 3-1/2 pence higher at 369-1/2.

Wessex said it would also buy back around 87 percent of a 19.5 percent stake held by its largest shareholder, Waste Management International Plc (WMI), at 355 pence per share. WMI said it would eventually sell all of its stake.
If both tenders are fully subscribed, Wessex will cut its capital by a quarter at a cost of around 240 million pounds ($400 million).
Wessex said ordinary shareholders would be able to sell a proportion of their shares but those with 200 shares or fewer would be able to sell all their holdings.

"We are giving our small shareholders the opportunity to sell all their shares and incur no dealing costs...and we shall also be having the opportunity, should we choose, of increasing dividends on an earnings per share basis," chairman Nicholas Hood said in a telephone interview.
Wessex said earlier this month it was looking into ways to boost shareholder benefits after a planned bid for South West Water was blocked by the government in October.

"We had been reserving our firepower for South West Water but as that was stopped...we believed the time had come to take account of our shareholders. This is a wish to run our balance sheet efficiently in an earnings-enhancing way," Hood said.

In a separate statement, Waste Management International, which bought a stake in Wessex in 1991 and established a Wessex Waste Management joint venture, said it was selling the stake to pump cash into its core business and cut debt.
The group said, however, that it remained committed to the joint venture with Wessex and its chairman Edwin Falkman would remain on Wessex's board as a non-executive director.

"Having cemented our relationship over these last several years, WMI determined that this was an appropriate time to free up the capital we have invested in Wessex," WMI chief executive Joseph Holsten said in a statement.
Hood said WMI's stake was rumoured to have been on the market for some time. "And I think that probably depressed our share price a bit," he added.
